title: Analysis of the accuracy and completeness of cardiovascular health information on alcohol industry-funded websites
screen_reason: Document and thematic analysis of 44 webpages (23 across 18 alcohol-industry/SAPRO websites, 21 across 18 non-industry-funded websites), accessed 24-30 June 2019. The study is largely qualitative; it reports one quantitative share, 9 of the 12 industry sources that mention cardiovascular impacts (75%) state that alcohol is associated with reduced risk of at least one cardiovascular condition. The coding instrument records only whether alcohol was described as a risk factor or as protective; no webpage was adjudicated true or false against a stated external ground truth, and the authors' accuracy verdict comes from the narrative discussion rather than from the coding. Under the QUALITY-vs-CONTENT test that makes this a QUALITY row, retained but excluded from prevalence.

estimates.country: International alcohol producers and social aspects organisations; comparison sites from the UK, USA, Ireland, Scotland, Australia and Canada
estimates.measure_type: % of alcohol-industry/SAPRO sources mentioning cardiovascular impacts that state alcohol is associated with reduced risk of at least one cardiovascular condition
estimates.value_raw: Of those 12, 9 (75%) state that alcohol consumption is associated with a reduced risk of at least one cardiovascular condition
estimates.denominator: 12 of the 18 alcohol-industry/SAPRO sources whose sampled webpages refer specifically to the cardiovascular impacts of drinking
estimates.definition: Webpage states that alcohol consumption is associated with a reduced risk of at least one cardiovascular condition (i.e. describes alcohol as protective rather than a risk factor)
estimates.misinfo_def: we hypothesized that AI/SAPRO websites were more likely to contain misleading or inaccurate representations of the risk to cardiovascular health from drinking

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors independently searched each webpage for eight named cardiovascular conditions and recorded whether alcohol was stated to be a risk factor or protective; 94.4% agreement, Cohen's kappa = 0.79. Thematic analysis by one author with a second re-reading for missed themes. No claim was scored against a stated accuracy standard or guideline.
estimates.moderator_quote: Firstly, each webpage was searched (independently, by two authors) for reference to MI; ischaemic (or coronary) heart disease; (congestive) heart failure; cardiomyopathy; hypertension; atrial fibrillation (or arrhythmia); peripheral vascular disease; and stroke (haemorrhagic or ischaemic). A distinction was drawn between 'myocardial infarction' and 'ischaemic heart disease' (which includes angina) due to evidence in the literature on the specific benefit to MI risk with moderate alcohol intake. Where a disease was mentioned, it was noted whether alcohol was stated to be a risk factor or pro- tective.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence, borderline. The label counts a claim type ('alcohol is protective for a cardiovascular condition'), not a falsity judgement: the authors themselves note evidence in the literature on a benefit to myocardial infarction risk at moderate intake, so a webpage could make this statement and not be wholly false. The authors' verdict that the industry 'misrepresents and understates' the harms comes from the narrative discussion, not from the coding rule. Purposive sample of the 18 leading IARD-member producers and industry-funded SAPROs, hence denom_selection=curated and population_scope=other (organisations, not individuals). Denominator is the 12 sources mentioning CVD, not the 18 sampled or the 23 webpages.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the counts in Table 2 and the text of how often each condition is mentioned (IHD 11 instances, alcohol described as protective on eight of these webpages; stroke n=17, hypertension n=16, MI or IHD n=14 for non-industry sites) — these are counts of mentions, not shares with a clean denominator, and the eight-of-eleven figure is a per-condition subset of the row above; (b) the five themes and ten sub-themes with their illustrative quotes, which are qualitative; (c) framing judgements (leading text supportive/negative/balanced), reported without numbers in the extracted text; (d) epidemiological background figures (5% of deaths secondary to alcohol, CVD over 25% of these) which are cited from elsewhere and not measures of misinformation. Worth a human's attention: the paper's title promises an accuracy analysis, but the only accuracy adjudication is narrative; no page is coded accurate or inaccurate, which is why I treated the 75% as QUALITY rather than CONTENT. The text file also contains trailing content from unrelated articles in the same journal issue (an oral-health/CLBP abstract), which I ignored.

rob.design: Document analysis of English-language websites, accessed 24-30 June 2019: 18 alcohol-industry/SAPRO sites (IARD members or affiliates, and SAPROs used in previous studies) and a comparison set of 18 government or non-industry-funded charity sites largely identified by prominence in country-specific Google searches; 44 webpages archived on Archive.Today (23 industry, 21 non-industry). Coding of disease mentions and risk/protective direction done independently by two authors, 94.4% agreement, Cohen's kappa = 0.79. Thematic analysis by one author with a second checking for missed themes. Reported against the SRQR checklist. Purposive, non-random sample; no accuracy adjudication in the coding scheme.
